name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,785

clue.text: Phosphorus, possibly an atom?

indicators.note: 'an' is only one example of the category ARTICLE, so the category is given by example

blocks.note: P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus
'an' is an indefinite article

explanation.surface: A chemistry question: could phosphorus be thought of as an atom?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that an atom is just one kind of particle. 'An' looks like a filler word; here it is an example of a grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an atom is one kind among many, and the question mark admits it.

clue.text: Help Dave's heart trouble

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle

blocks.note: the middle two letters of DAVE
to ail = to trouble, as an illness does

explanation.surface: A plea to help Dave with his heart problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart trouble' reads as a medical phrase, but 'heart' belongs with Dave and 'trouble' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail is to help or be of use, as in 'it availed him nothing'.

clue.text: Seniors note park runs are ruthless

indicators.note: the letters run about into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

explanation.surface: Pensioners observe that the runners in a weekend park run are merciless.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface leans on parkrun, the free weekly timed 5k held in parks, so 'park runs' looks like a single noun. 'Runs' is the verb that stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To take no prisoners is to act without mercy or compromise, that is, to be ruthless.

clue.text: Last car in America has shorter boot in case

indicators.note: the word is made shorter by losing its last letter
the cut-down word goes in the other one

blocks.note: the outer word, split around the insert: CA...SE
BOOT without its final T

explanation.surface: An American car with a cramped boot to put your luggage in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last car' sounds like the final model a maker built; it is the last wagon of a train, the caboose in American usage (a guard's van in Britain).
explanation.definitionFit: A caboose is the car at the end of an American freight train.

clue.text: Old mare wanders grand estate

indicators.note: the letters wander out of their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: An elderly horse roams freely across the lands of a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand estate' sounds like parkland for the horse to roam; it is the rank and lands that go with a noble title.
explanation.definitionFit: An earldom is the territory held by an earl, a grand estate.

clue.text: Hard like that hat

blocks.note: so = in that way, as in 'do it so'
lid is informal for a hat

explanation.surface: A hard hat, described in the terse way of a shop label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard ... hat' calls up a builder's helmet, but 'Hard' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Solid and hard both mean firm and not yielding to pressure.

clue.text: Veggie meal range is in Latvian store finally

indicators.note: take only the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a span is a range, as in a time span
used as it stands
at home = in, as in 'is she in?'
a Lett is a Latvian person
last letter of STORE

explanation.surface: A vegetarian food range is on sale in a Latvian shop at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a positional link, but it is a word in its own right: HOME, as in 'staying in'. LETT is an old word for a Latvian.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish omelette of potato, egg and onion is a meat-free meal.

clue.text: Walkers' home large and cool amid spreading trees

indicators.note: the cool word sits in the middle of the others
the trees spread out into a new order

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels
TREES rearranged, split E...STER around the insert
to ice = to cool

explanation.surface: Hikers live in a big, shady house among wide-spreading trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walkers' suggests hikers; it is Walkers, the British crisp maker, whose main factory is in Leicester, an English city.
explanation.definitionFit: Walkers crisps are made in Leicester, so the city is their home.

clue.text: Kebab almost sufficiently cooked

indicators.note: almost all of the word: drop its last letter

blocks.note: the spit-roast Turkish kebab, minus its final letter R

explanation.surface: A kebab that is nearly cooked enough to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: A doner kebab is often just called a doner in Britain. The surface has 'almost' qualifying the cooking; it trims the kebab instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain kitchen synonym: a steak is 'done' once cooked to the degree wanted.

clue.text: Sons want less busy time

blocks.note: S = son, the genealogical abbreviation
want = lack, as in 'for want of'

explanation.surface: The boys would like a quieter period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as desire, but here it means the lack of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Slack is a quiet period with little business, as in 'a slack season'.

clue.text: Fish pie's crust coated with fish

indicators.note: a pie's crust is its outside, so take the outer letters
the outer letters are coated, wrapped round, by the other word

blocks.note: the second 'fish', a verb: to fish for = to search for, split SEA...RCH around the insert
first and last letters of PIE

explanation.surface: A fish pie whose pastry is topped with more fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'fish' is a verb, meaning to search, not another fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea perch is a name for various sea fish such as the bass.

clue.text: Uncivilised local lawyers, many naked on island

indicators.note: stripped of its outer letters
in an across clue, placed after the island

blocks.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, which has a bar
the Bar is the body of barristers
I = island, as on maps
MANY without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Rough local lawyers, lots of them nude, on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is the British word for one's nearest pub, not an adjective for the lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbarian as an adjective means uncivilised or savage.

clue.text: Ready to drop ball soon enough

blocks.note: all in = exhausted
having a ball = having a good time

explanation.surface: Someone is poised to let go of a ball any moment now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready to drop' reads as about to release the ball; it means worn out. 'Ball' is the fun you have at one, not the object.
explanation.definitionFit: All in good time means it will happen soon enough, so be patient.

clue.text: Plane carrying meals not able to provide sandwiches

indicators.note: the words enclose the answer like bread round a filling

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'not' through 'able' and 'to' into the start of 'provide'

explanation.surface: An airliner with a food service that cannot offer sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' is not an aircraft but a flat surface; the airline scene is a decoy. 'Sandwiches' is a verb, hiding the answer between its neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabletop is a flat surface on which meals are set.

clue.text: Hide prunes inside empty envelope

indicators.note: the first word goes inside the second
an emptied word keeps only its outer letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of ENVELOPE, split E...E
to prune = to clip

explanation.surface: Instructions for concealing some dried plums in an empty envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prunes' looks like the fruit; it is the verb, to trim.
explanation.definitionFit: To eclipse something is to block it from view, to hide it.

clue.text: Embarrassing marks, when you suck at subject you like?

definitions.text: when you suck at subject you like?

blocks.note: the bruises left by kissing and sucking skin

blocks.clueFragment: when you suck at subject you like?
blocks.note: read as slang: what you adore is rubbish, it 'bites'

explanation.surface: A pupil's embarrassing grades in a favourite subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' suggests school grades, and 'suck at' suggests being bad at a subject. Read slangily, 'love bites' is a sentence: your love is lousy. The question mark flags the pun; 'suck' also points at how the bruises are made.
explanation.definitionFit: Love bites are bruises from kissing, usually embarrassing to show.

clue.text: Wise man that has time off initially, between degrees

indicators.note: the time letter comes off at the start
the result sits between the two degrees

blocks.note: two MAs, Masters of Arts, split MA...MA around the insert
THAT with its first letter, T for time, removed

explanation.surface: A sage who takes early leave, sitting between two university courses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time off' looks like a holiday; T for time is what comes off.
explanation.definitionFit: A mahatma is a revered sage, the title given to Gandhi.

clue.text: Volume drunk by cold climbers not uniform

definitions.note: 'not uniform' works as 'what you wear when not in uniform'

indicators.note: swallowed, so the V goes inside

blocks.note: C = cold, as on taps
ivies are climbing plants; split IV...IES around the insert
V = volume

explanation.surface: A quantity of drink downed by chilly mountaineers not in regulation gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbers' are plants, not mountaineers. Civvies is British slang for civilian clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Civvies are ordinary clothes worn off duty, as opposed to uniform.

clue.text: Sergeant-major carries one close

indicators.note: the outer letters carry the rest inside

blocks.note: SM = sergeant-major; split S...M around the insert
I = one, the Roman numeral
close = dear, as in a close friend

explanation.surface: A sergeant-major keeps something near at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: what a sergeant-major carries close to him is a sidearm.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidearm is a pistol worn at the side, kept close by an officer.

clue.text: Gold parts most womanly, like thighs

definitions.note: 'like thighs' stands for 'of thighs', an adjective

indicators.note: gold parts the other word, pushing into it
most of the word, dropping its last letter

blocks.note: FEMALE without its last letter, split FEM...AL around the insert
or = gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Gilded body parts, with the most feminine thighs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most womanly' looks like a superlative; 'most' means most of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Femoral means relating to the thigh or thighbone.

clue.text: Outbreak from feral bats ahead

indicators.note: bats = crazy, so the letters go mad

blocks.note: FERAL rearranged
up = ahead, as in 'two goals up'

explanation.surface: A disease outbreak traced to wild bats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' reads as the animals; it is the adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A flare-up is a sudden outbreak, of violence or illness.

clue.text: Mad dog had a trilby, for the midday sun?

indicators.note: mad = crazed, and a crazed jumble of letters loses its original order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: A crazed dog wears a hat to go out at noon.
explanation.walkthrough: An echo of Noel Coward's song 'Mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun'. A trilby is a soft felt hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The midday sun gives broad daylight, the full light of day.

clue.text: Reptile somewhat resembling a tortoise

indicators.note: only some of the words are used

blocks.note: the letters sit across the end of 'resembling', all of 'a' and the start of 'tortoise'

explanation.surface: A reptile that looks a bit like a tortoise.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literally true, which hides the fact that the answer is sitting in the words.
explanation.definitionFit: An American clipping: the reptile's full name shortened to its last two syllables.

clue.text: Flat and broad cakes that must be flipped

indicators.note: turned over, so read backwards

blocks.note: buns are small cakes

explanation.surface: Pancakes, flat and wide, that need turning in the pan.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is pancakes; 'flipped' is the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A snub nose is short and flat, broad rather than pointed.

clue.text: Church wine, never dull bottles

indicators.note: dull bottles the wine, holding it inside

blocks.note: no = never, as in 'no way'
tame = dull, unexciting; split T...AME around the insert
red wine

explanation.surface: A verdict on communion wine: the bottles are never dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun for the wine; it is the verb, to contain.
explanation.definitionFit: Notre-Dame is the great cathedral church in Paris.

clue.text: Calculate maximum that trade union will accept? On the contrary

indicators.note: one word takes the other inside it
swap the roles: the maximum takes in the union, not the other way round

blocks.note: top = maximum, as in top speed; split TO...P around the insert
TU = trade union

explanation.surface: Work out the highest pay offer a union will accept, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read plainly, the union accepts the maximum; 'On the contrary' flips who holds whom.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal phrasal synonym: 'tot' comes from 'total', so the phrase means working out a sum.

clue.text: Reason guitar clamps fit centrally

indicators.note: the guitar clamps the letter inside it
centrally = at the centre, so only the centre letter of the word is used

blocks.note: a bass guitar; split BAS...S around the insert
middle letter of FIT

explanation.surface: Why guitar clamps fit in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clamps' reads as a noun, gear for a guitarist; it is the verb, to grip.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: 'on what grounds?' and 'for what reason?' ask the same thing.

clue.text: Yep, Trump oozes incompetence

indicators.note: the letters ooze out in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A political jibe: yes, Trump reeks of incompetence.
explanation.walkthrough: A muppet is British slang for a fool, so muppetry is foolish incompetence.
explanation.definitionFit: Muppetry is bungling, the behaviour of a muppet.
